> 持而盈之，不如其已；揣而銳之，不可長保。

Chapter 9 is about the hardest moment in any successful endeavor: not the struggle, but the morning after.

Five lines, one slope:

1. Hold a cup full and keep filling — stop instead.
2. Hammer an edge sharp and keep sharpening — it won't last.
3. Gold and jade fill the hall — no one can guard it.
4. Wealth and rank with arrogance — self-inflicted fault.
5. The work is done, the self withdraws — this is the way of heaven.

Each is the same structure at a different scale: 把自我綁在所得上 — tying the self to what has been obtained. The tighter the binding, the faster the fall.

## 持而盈之

盈 is not fullness as satisfaction; it is fullness as the refusal to stop. The problem is not that the cup is full — a full cup is fine — it is that the hand keeps pouring, because stopping would mean accepting that the current level is the level.

Anyone who has shipped something knows this state. The release is out, and instead of resting, you keep adding one more feature, because the moment you stop, the thing becomes finite and therefore judgeable.

## 揣而銳之

揣 is to hammer, to forge an edge. 銳 is the sharpness that gets admired. The line says: it cannot be kept.

Not because sharpness is bad, but because sharpness is a maintenance debt. The sharper the edge, the more of your attention goes into protecting it, and the attention comes out of the work the edge was for.

## 金玉滿堂，莫之能守

This one is usually read as a warning about greed. It is more specific: the problem is not the amount, it is the 守 — the assumption that possession is a stable state.

Nothing that can be held is held permanently. The hall full of jade requires guards, inventories, heirs, and a story about why it's yours. The guarding becomes the occupation, and the thing guarded stops being used.

## 功遂身退

This is the line that gets read as retirement, resignation, or sour grapes. It says none of those.

功遂 — the work is accomplished. 身退 — the self withdraws. What withdraws is not the person from the work, but the self from the achievement.

The distinction is precise: 退 is not leaving the project; it is not moving your center of gravity into the result. The work is done, and the "I" does not take up residence in it, does not require the result to keep saying something about its author.

Read this way, 天之道 is not a rule about timing. It is the same 不自生 from chapter 7: the thing that does not organize itself around its own continuation can continue.

## Why this is the hard chapter

Chapters 1 through 8 train seeing and acting. Chapter 9 trains the aftermath, and the aftermath is where most people lose what they built — not to enemies, but to the maintenance of their own position.

功遂身退 offers the only exit that doesn't require either false modesty or endless defense: let the work be the work, and don't move in.

## A test

Name one result you are still defending. Ask what would happen if you simply stopped mentioning it for a month. The answer usually tells you how much of your current effort is 守 and how little is 用.
